HIRING: Energetic Materials Expert for Redteaming

Rate: $65–$75 per task
Type: Contract, Remote

About the Work:
Mercor is assembling a panel of explosives and energetic materials experts to red-team frontier AI models. The goal is to test whether a model can correctly judge the misuse potential of a technical request – answering legitimate questions fully while refusing genuinely dangerous ones.

What You'll Do:
Write challenging single-turn prompts in your domain, labelled across three levels: benign, dual-use, and adversarial
Evaluate responses against a defined policy standard and judge whether each was handled correctly
Write the reference answer – what a correct response looks like and the technical reasoning for why

Background We're Looking For (both profiles needed):
Chemists with specialty materials expertise:
Specialty Materials Chemist (pyrotechnics or propulsion) – formulation, synthesis, performance testing
Federal Certified Materials Specialist / Incident Analyst – forensic identification and scene analysis
Engineers/operators with initiation and propulsion system experience:
Hazardous Device Specialist / Public Safety Professional – render-safe procedures and device assessment
Propulsion & Effects Engineer – munitions and propulsion system design
Commercial Blasting Engineer – specialty materials handling, storage, and transport
Prior AI evaluation or red-teaming experience is preferred.

What This Role Demands:
This is writing-intensive work. Every judgment needs a written rationale that a non-specialist can follow. Prior technical writing, incident or post-blast reporting, published research, or expert witness experience is a strong signal – please include a sample or link.
You will be reading and writing about misuse scenarios in your field for sustained periods. Experts are briefed in advance, and you can pause or step away at any point without penalty.

Important:
Your work must not draw on classified or export-controlled information, or anything covered by an NDA or prepublication review obligation. If you hold such obligations, you may still be a good fit – tell us in your application and we'll scope the work accordingly.

Apply here: https://t.mercor.com/oYWFK

Another great trip out to Copenhagen.

I genuinely thought that after my 20th trip I'd eventually get bored of the city, but I think I enjoy it more every time I visit. (Especially when the sun decides to show up.)

Last week we met with 107 different people across the Danish market. As always, the conversations were insightful, honest and a great reminder of why face-to-face meetings still matter (and are a USP that will beat AI in our industry). 

Some of the key themes that came up:
✅ AI
✅ Scaling teams and projects heading into Q4
✅ New contract opportunities
✅ Building more efficient hiring processes
✅ And... AI again


Outside of AI, there is still a huge amount of optimism in the market. Many businesses are preparing for a strong finish to 2026, with hiring plans becoming clearer and project demand increasing across several sectors.

Looking forward to seeing what Q4 brings.

More often than not, when we talk flexible hiring models like embedded talent with a founder or a people leader, we are met with a “we didn’t even know that was an option.”
 
 Which is odd, because the market is moving in exactly the direction embedded was built for: fast growth, uneven hiring, and no appetite for a permanent talent team you might not need in eighteen months.
  
The money there, but it's picking favourites. Gallagher Re put Q2 insurtech funding at $2.44bn, the highest quarter since 2022, with 99.1% going to AI-focused businesses. Early-stage funding fell by more than half. So some scale-ups are about to hire in bursts they've never had to manage before, and everyone else is chasing the same people with a fraction of the budget. Neither problem is solved by a job ad and an agency terms sheet.
  
Time to fill is now a strategic risk. AWS reckons filling an AI role in UK financial services takes nine months, up from five and a half. Decide you need a team today and it's in seat by summer 2027. Most business plans don't wait that long.
  
And what firms can't find isn't engineers. ManpowerGroup found the hardest skill for UK employers to find is basic AI literacy, and only one in ten is using AI to cut heads. The people-leader job in 2027 is less about shrinking headcount and more about what the existing headcount can do.
  
So, embedded talent, what is it? A recruiter or small team that sits inside your business for a fixed period, on your systems, in your meetings, hiring as you rather than for you. You get the pace and market reach of an agency with the knowledge and accountability of an in-house team, and you switch it off when the burst is over. Tech scale-ups have used it for years. In insurance and insurtech, plenty of leaders are hearing about it for the first time.
  
Where we'd put energy if we were running a growing insurance or insurtech business right now:
  
(1) Work out which of your next 20 hires are a burst and which are a steady drip. They need different models, and one agency contract won't serve both.
  
(2) Build AI literacy into the roles you already have before you open a req for a head of AI. Cheaper, faster, and it fixes the bigger gap.
  
(3) Know your options before you need them. Agency, RPO, embedded, MSP, talent advisory. If you can only name two of those, you're choosing from half the menu.
  
That last one is the whole point of this post. Know the model exists for what you need before the burst hits.

Want to chat it through? Reach out to Santa Brown

Every AI vendor demo looks good because that's the point of a demo.

The demo uses their best data, a workflow they've run a hundred times, and a use case chosen to look good. What it doesn't show you is how the product actually behaves when it's running on your data, answering your customers' questions, in your actual setup.

Gartner surveyed 782 infrastructure and operations leaders in late 2025. Only 28% said their AI projects fully met ROI expectations. One in five failed outright. That gap almost always starts in the vendor evaluation stage.

Three things worth doing before signing anything.

- Ask for a pilot with your actual data. If you're evaluating an AI chatbot vendor, don't let them demo it on their own sample queries. Give them a real batch of your support tickets and ask them to show you how it handles them. Same with an AI hiring tool - run it on your actual job descriptions and real applications. The vendor who stalls on this is telling you something. The one who says yes immediately is worth talking to further.

- Ask what the product cannot do. An AI analytics vendor once told a founder I know that their tool could "handle any data source." Three months into the contract, it couldn't connect to their CRM. Good vendors tell you where their product falls short before you discover it yourself. If a vendor can only talk about what the product does well, that's performative.

- Read the contract before you get excited. AI contracts right now routinely include auto-renewal clauses with 90-day notice windows. Performance metrics defined by the vendor, not you. Vague language around what happens to your data after you leave. None of these are in there because they benefit you.

The evaluation stage is the cheapest time to find out a vendor isn't right.

Workday has won the right to keep its bias testing secret. That should unsettle you more than a loss would have.

Derek Mobley applied to more than a hundred jobs through Workday's hiring platform. He was rejected every time. He sued the vendor rather than the employers. Thousands of applicants have since joined him.

Three years in, the fight is still not about whether the software discriminated. It is about whether anyone gets to look.

In May a magistrate judge held that Workday's bias testing is privileged. The code, the data, the results. Workday's lawyers had curated the inputs, chosen the comparisons, and kept the findings away from any regulator. That structure is what made it privileged. The district judge let it stand in June. A separate ruling spared Workday from producing detailed records of the applications the platform processed.

The claimants cannot reach the evidence that would prove the claim.

Now read that as a buyer.

If the bias testing belongs to your vendor's counsel, you never see it either. You cannot request it. It is not your file and not your privilege to waive.

And you still carry the deployer obligations.

Here is why this lands now rather than in 2027.

Europe has moved the high-risk deadline for AI in recruitment out to December 2027. Ireland signed its implementing legislation into law on 21 July and stood up an AI Office to enforce it.

So you have roughly fifteen months. So does every vendor in the market. And they have just been handed a blueprint for putting their bias testing beyond reach.

The question is what you build in that window.

If the answer is a vendor assurance pack and a signed contract, you arrive in December 2027 in the position the Mobley claimants are in now. Certain something happened. Unable to see how.

Every AI decision is a leadership decision wearing a technology costume. 🧭

What if AI isn't coming for your job… but for the broken parts of recruitment?
We spend a lot of time debating whether AI will replace humans. Perhaps we're asking the wrong question.
Over the past eight months, I've gone through #recruitment processes with a couple of US-based companies, including micro1, and I've been genuinely impressed by how deeply they've integrated AI - from interviewing through to onboarding.

The #interview itself was conducted by an #AI agent trained to assess my responses against the theoretical & practical requirements of the job.
And honestly? It was more engaging than some interviews I've had with actual humans who seemed to have only a half-baked understanding of the role or the person they were interviewing. But what impressed me most was the speed & transparency. The entire process can happen within 3–10 days. #Candidates can track their #application and, if unsuccessful, request detailed feedback.

Within 24 hours, the AI can provide specific feedback on strengths & areas for improvement. Compare that with the traditional process:
Apply.
Wait.
Interview.
Wait some more.
Follow up.
Wait again.
Then receive:
"Thank you for your application. Unfortunately..."
Sometimes after two or three months.

No meaningful feedback. No development points. Just rejection.
Interestingly, I haven't secured every contract I've applied for through these platforms. But I walked away knowing exactly what I needed to improve. In some cases, I wasn't giving the wrong answers. I simply wasn't providing enough practical detail around the expected outcomes.

That's valuable.
Rejection became development to #research and improve. I've rarely been actually challenged by interviews, and FYI, #creatives love engaging interviews. 
That's where I think AI could fundamentally change recruitment.
AI can handle screening, scheduling, structured interviews, assessments, application tracking and feedback—tasks that consume enormous amounts of human time but don't necessarily require human judgment.

If AI can give #hiring managers back 50–75% of that time, perhaps they can spend more of it doing what humans actually do best:
Understanding people.
Assessing character.
Exploring cultural fit.
Building relationships.
Making nuanced decisions.
Of course, AI has limitations. Personality, emotional intelligence, chemistry & other human characteristics aren't always captured by algorithms.

So perhaps the future isn't AI replacing humans.
Perhaps it's AI removing the robotic parts of hiring so humans can focus on the human parts. And that raises an uncomfortable question:
If AI can make recruitment faster, more transparent and more useful to candidates, why are we so determined to preserve a system that often isn't?
Maybe the future of hiring isn't Humans vs AI.
Maybe it's simply:
AI doing what machines do best. Humans doing what humans do best. And perhaps that's not the death of human capital.
Perhaps it's an opportunity to finally use it properly.

Are we seeing the return of the Tech Contractor?

The latest market data suggests we might be. IT contractor demand has picked up, while permanent hiring remains a more cautious market and when you look at what businesses are still trying to deliver, it makes sense.

AI programmes.
Cloud transformation.
Cyber security.
Data projects.
ERP and digital transformation.

The projects haven’t gone away, but with businesses continuing to keep a close eye on headcount and budgets, the way those projects are being resourced is changing.

We’re seeing more consideration around bringing in specialist contractors who can deliver a specific piece of work, provide additional capacity or bring expertise that simply isn't available internally. For the right project, that can make a lot of sense.

You’re bringing in someone who has done it before, understands the environment and can add value from day one , without necessarily making a long-term headcount commitment.

Of course, contractors aren't the answer to every hiring challenge. There are roles where permanent talent is absolutely the right solution. But I think we’ll continue to see businesses take a more blended approach to technology hiring, building permanent capability where they need it, while using specialist contractors to support transformation, delivery and periods of increased demand.

At Savant, we recruit across both contract and permanent technology, so we’re seeing first-hand how those conversations are changing. For me, it’s less about contract versus permanent and more about choosing the right talent model for what the business needs to deliver.
That’s an interesting shift in the market, and one I expect we’ll see more of over the coming months.

If you’re seeing something similar in your business, let’s have a natter over a coffee. ☕

A post landed on my feed today that had the comments section in a bit of a spin. Anthropic, the company behind Claude, is hiring a Senior Recruiting Coordinator on a 12 month contract at just over $120,000 a year. Half the comments were some version of "can't they just get an agent to do that?" and the other half were people enjoying the irony, given most of us have spent two years being told AI is coming for recruitment.
 
I went and read the actual spec, which I'd recommend before anyone settles into the irony, because it doesn't say what people think it says.
 
The role isn't booking interviews. The automation already does that bit. The role is supervising the automation, setting it up, checking what comes out of it before a candidate ever sees it, and deciding when a loop needs a person rather than the automated path. There's a line about owning the recovery when the automation gets something wrong, and another about knowing when to trust the output and when to override it.
 
So what they've built is a recruitment job designed around the tooling rather than in spite of it, where the value sits in judging the work instead of doing it.
 
That's the part worth sitting with, because the same shift is coming for the rest of us. Nobody is going to pay a fee for a search anyone can run in thirty seconds. They'll pay for the person who knows the client's shift patterns, who can hear when a candidate's answer doesn't quite add up, who picks the phone up at four on a Friday when the process wobbles and 40 people need to be on site Monday morning.
 
The tools will take the admin, and good riddance to most of it. The judgement is still the job, and I'd argue it's worth more now than it was five years ago.
 
Did anyone else read the spec, or just the headline?

"Data centres do not create many jobs."
 
That line is doing the rounds again this week, and on a headcount per megawatt basis it is not wrong. A 100MW site can run on a few dozen people once it is live.
 
What the headline misses is what those few dozen people actually do.
 
⚡ A NOC engineer covering a site overnight is the difference between a five minute blip and an SLA breach
 🖥️ A rack and stack crew landing 2,000 GPUs inside a fixed window is the difference between capacity going live this quarter or next
 🌐 A network engineer bringing up the fabric between those GPUs decides whether the cluster performs like one machine or a very expensive room full of them
 
Small teams. Enormous leverage per head. And the hiring happens in bursts around go lives, migrations and refreshes, not on a steady drumbeat.
 
That is why so much of it runs on contract as well as permanent. One engineer for a single fit out, or a full crew on a longer programme, then back to a lean core team.
 
Job numbers are a poor measure of what a data centre means to the people who run it. Leverage per engineer is the better one.
 
At TTC Group we place the engineers behind the AI infrastructure layer: data centre operations, networks, GPU and HPC, on contract and permanent. If that is the layer you run, let's connect.

We’re back to school (and work! but isn’t that kind of the same thing?) in France, and I’ve now realized — we’re 3 years into Versant. Whoa.

Since starting out, we’ve witnessed the rise of AI systems, and how they have become ubiquitous in how we interact with the digital world. This is a trend, and maybe it’s a bubble, but the effects of bubbles stay. And that’s what we’re building for — the reality of how we will get work done from now until, well, the next thing.

This has immensely affected our technical direction. We began with helping project developers with the surprisingly difficult problem of finding land for ecological compensation. Before we arrived with our tools to model species suitability, wetland probability, and additionality in parcels around a project area - project developers were largely flying blind, or having to contract with consultancies who had to do a ton of manual work. We unblocked them, and we did that without AI.

But now with AI… Wow. We can do a lot more. Putting aside the boost it has given us on our development cycles, we learned we can do some really interesting stuff to help with compliance. Where before there was regulatory roadblocks and speedbumps, our systems are now able to help construction developers navigate them with ease; while maintaining our goal of protecting and preserving biodiversity.

I often see people complaining on LinkedIn about how European regulations stifle innovation. Well, some of them sure are annoying, but I think many can provide interesting opportunities to build tools and companies to truly enable sustainable growth.

I’m happily biased. Also, we’re hiring. 😉

The biggest trap in global delivery management is confusing geographical expansion with capability maturity.

Adding 500 engineering seats in a capability hub does not make an enterprise more innovative if the operating model still treats the team as a remote typing pool.

Zinnov-Nasscom benchmarks show India is now the world's leading AI talent hub with 506,000 AI/ML professionals across GCCs. But hiring talent without granting decision rights simply accelerates talent churn.

The structural divide between offshore cost hubs and enterprise nerve centres:

The Cost-Arbitrage Hub (Legacy GCC 1.0 and 2.0):
- Strategic Mandate: Processing transactional back-office tickets and executing routine runbooks
- Primary Value Metric: Hourly labor rate differentials, seat utilization, and localized cost savings
- Decision Authority: Order-taker execution with zero strategic roadmap or budget ownership
- AI and Automation: Fragmented prompt pilots and isolated chatbots without enterprise data rails
- Organizational Posture: Subordinate offshore cost center vulnerable to vendor consolidation
- Talent Retention: High attrition driven by repetitive transactional tasks and flat career ladders

The Enterprise Nerve Centre (Next-Gen GCC 3.0):
- Strategic Mandate: Leading global digital transformation, core platform engineering, and AI architecture
- Primary Value Metric: Commercial impact, operating margin acceleration, and proprietary IP creation
- Decision Authority: End-to-end product, technology, and operational P&L ownership with board visibility
- AI and Automation: Production multi-agent systems and real-time event streams driving core workflows
- Organizational Posture: Autonomous transformation engine setting global operating standards
- Talent Retention: High retention powered by deep domain ownership, technical rigor, and leadership pathways

You cannot build an AI-first enterprise on top of a 2005 offshore governance model.

Leading transformation executives redesign the operating contract: they grant GCCs full lifecycle ownership of strategic platforms, embed robust AI guardrails, and tie delivery directly to enterprise P&L results.

Which core enterprise capabilities has your organization successfully transitioned to full ownership within your global delivery hubs?
